  • A mathematician at Anthropic has said that the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most notable unsolved problems in mathematics – and experts say the claim checks out.
  • Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge notes it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis.

A mathematician at Anthropic has said that the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most notable unsolved problems in mathematics – and experts say the claim checks out.

Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks.

On Saturday afternoon, two organizations announced that they had independently verified Alpöge’s claim after reviewing the programming language he used to share the solution.

The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems.

Sources indicate that “Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”.

Alpöge linked to computer code – written in a language called Lean – that he maintained could verify the findings.

Mathematicians subsequently began working to see if Alpöge’s proof could be confirmed. On Saturday afternoon, the Lean Focused Research Organization – which seeks to advance the use of the programming language – and the Mathlib Initiative, a program that works with Lean for math equations, confirmed that they had verified Alpöge’s solution.

“We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the groups announced.

Recent findings suggest that alpöge’s note was published just one day after Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. He acknowledged that, writing: “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier.”.

The Riemann hypothesis is a nearly 170-year-old math problem named after Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician who proposed it in 1859.

The hypothesis deals with prime numbers – whole numbers greater than 1 that can only be divided by themselves and 1. Riemann questioned how often prime numbers appear and how they are distributed along the number line. And he developed a formula for estimating how many prime numbers exist under a specific number.

Sources indicate that the Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium prize math problems selected in 200 by the Clay Mathematics Institute. The institute has offered $1m for each problem solved.

Industry observers note that mathematicians have been attempting to solve this problem for years. The Latest York Times reported that on Friday, an independent mathematician in Italy released an incomplete proof of the Riemann hypothesis that he noted he had been working on for almost 12 years. That mathematician, Alessandro Masullo, said he did not use AI because he did not fully trust the system.

Other mathematicians have expressed discomfort with relying on AI to solve math problems.

It has been revealed that in September, Anthropic competitor OpenAI claimed that a non-public version of its AI tools helped solve part of another Millennium prize problem. But it was solved in a way that struck mathematicians and observers in a way many found strange: a near-trillion-dollar private organization spent $15m to employ 10,000 AI systems to solve the problem.

Alpöge was working on that separate problem for Anthropic when OpenAI made its announcement.

University of Warwick mathematician James Robinson told the Guardian in September that “it’s frustrating to see these major tech companies burning this fuel up just so that they can show off about how great their latest model is”.

He added: “It seems like immature playground boasting writ large, underpinned by billions of dollars and the potential for significant environmental damage in an age when climate change is probably the biggest challenge we face.”.

Walmart mentioned global e-commerce sales surged 17% in the fiscal third quarter, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter.

Walmart noted it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices.

CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the company has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices.

Industry observers note that "The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner noted in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can.".

Industry observers note that CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter.

"This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses.".

Walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey said Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.

Sources indicate that walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth.

Here's how the firm performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Industry observers note that for the quarter ended Oct. 31, the tech giant reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%.

Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share.

Industry observers note that walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.

Furner also said Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

"It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he said.

In a recent development, sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It said its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise.

It has been revealed that in October, Walmart declared it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer stand-alone memberships, as well.

According to recent reports, furner told CNBC the new membership has brought roughly 2 million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the organization reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more.".

The tech giant on Thursday mentioned its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.

The company is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company mentioned it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef.

Rainey said Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start.".

The massive-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

  • Voters go to the polls in the village of Castle Bromwich in the West Midlands on Thursday in a little-noticed election that is the latest test for Reform at a time when it is particularly vulnerable.
  • Yet, while it is the Conservatives who are edging ahead in recent polls, the decisive difference could well be the performance of Restore Britain – the hard-right party set up by Rupert Lowe after the MP fell out with Nigel Farage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thursday’s byelection in Castle Bromwich will be latest test for Nigel Farage’s party as rival eats into support.

Voters go to the polls in the village of Castle Bromwich in the West Midlands on Thursday in a little-noticed election that is the latest test for Reform at a time when it is particularly vulnerable.

Yet, while it is the Conservatives who are edging ahead in recent polls, the decisive difference could well be the performance of Restore Britain – the hard-right party set up by Rupert Lowe after the MP fell out with Nigel Farage.

Reform has lost no less than five elections since September, on one occasion by as little as two votes, after Restore attracted voters who might otherwise have voted for Farage’s party.

Industry observers note that the possibility of offering an electoral pact to Restore is now under discussion among some figures at Reform’s Millbank HQ, the Guardian understands. There is also fervent internal opposition from some who balk at the ethno-nationalism that has found a home in Restore.

“Just take a look at some of the people who have attached themselves to Restore, as well as what some of their people have said about Jews and Muslims in their comments,” said one.

At the same time, and even after an aborted attempt to bury the hatchet between Lowe and Farage, others in Reform are leaving the door open to a reconciliation with Restore at a time when the party needs to find a way to overcome its stalling support.

“There’s an argument that we should be going after Restore and we’ll benefit from that, but there is also one where we work with them … and, to be honest, I don’t know the answer yet,” said one.

One senior Reform source noted the idea of a “non-aggression pact” with Restore was in the air and there was a “deal to be done” but was more sceptical about a deeper tie up or merger.

At the same time, other senior Reform figures who are close to Farage are pushing for him to go much further towards a detente with Rupert Lowe, with efforts under way to push them back together.

Among Reform insiders, there is an acknowledgment that Farage is at least as exercised and frustrated about Restore eating into the party’s vote as he is about the investigations into his own financial affairs. One Reform politician noted they envisaged Lowe ultimately being readmitted, but that the price would be the exit of Zia Yusuf, who had accused Lowe of assaulting him amid the furore that led to the MP’s suspension from the party.

In a recent development, however, that was before Yusuf this week appeared to praise Lowe in a conversation with the Spectator’s editor, Michael Gove. “Rupert is a force of nature,” mentioned Yusuf, who went on to describe him as a “formidable person” in comments that drew a strikingly warm response from Lowe himself, who tweeted that he appreciated Yusuf’s acknowledgment of Restore’s progress.

“I suspect on policy and trust in politics, Yusuf and I have more in common than the former Tory ministers in Reform’s leadership,” he added.

Last week, there was a public display of Reform working with Restore when the former Tory MPs Andrew Rosindell and Suella Braverman signed an early day motion by Lowe opposing a Liberal Democrat bid to pave the way for census questions to include more ethnicity options to allow people to define themselves as Black English or Asian English.

Even within Restore, and away from the public rhetoric, there is curiosity about the openness of Reform to some form of pact as the speculation about an early general election persists.

“Our offer remains on the table and we are open to negotiating that offer,” said a Restore source, who cited events in the summer when it looked like a reconciliation between Farage and Lowe was in the offing.

“It is Farage and others who have outright rejected it, but the ball is in their court.”.

On that occasion, what seemed like tentative moves towards peace broke down amid a fresh row between the two leaders, with Lowe accusing Farage of lying after the latter had noted he had reached out but had not heard back.

What remains clear now though is that Restore’s consistent nudging of 5% in serious national polls has taken some in its own ranks and even in Reform – whose leader predicted that its rival “would be lucky to get 1% anywhere” – by surprise. A Restore source noted of Reform: “It feels like they’re having a bit of an identity crisis and falling below 20% has clearly given them pause for thought.”.

More stark has been the proliferation of Restore branches across the UK – sometimes numbering just a handful of people but in others much larger – and the steady dripfeed of defections from Reform.

Last week, those who joined Lowe at a lavish central London dinner for members of Restore’s “Cromwell Club” for those donating £2,500 a year included Holly Vallance, the estranged wife of Reform’s honorary treasurer Nick Candy, who had frequently been cited as a potential candidate for Farage’s party.

Also there was Charlton Edwards, who was Reform’s treasurer until recently and a figure at the very heart of the courting of donors by Farage’s party.

Aside from the beef between Farage and Lowe – arguably the biggest alpha males on the right – the biggest stumbling block to a pact is the antisemitism within Restore, noted one source in Reform, which has made a concerted effort to court the British Jewish community.

Recent findings suggest that “Restore emerged because Rupert was out for revenge and it’s hard to ignore. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, amazon redesigned its Kindle e-reader for 2026, and it now includes a removable back panel, allowing consumers to replace the battery more easily. As much as we like the idea of a repairable Kindle, Mashable's testing revealed that the back panel can come off accidentally when removing the Kindle from its case, exposing the internal components.

It has been revealed that customers have taken notice of this design flaw, too. A Reddit user also reported the back of their Kindle popping off with minor pressure, and so did TikTok user Jackie's Book Tally, who posted a video of the latest Kindle coming apart while removing it from the case. So far, we've only encountered reports of this problem on the base Kindle and Kindle Paperwhite models.

Since originally publishing our report about the back of the upcoming Kindles popping off, we asked Mashable readers to let us know if they've experienced this issue, and we heard from one reader who mentioned he did.

Mashable reader Simon Forster reached out with photos of his 2026 Kindle Paperwhite. He remarked that after taking it out of its case, the back popped off unexpectedly, fully exposing the back elements. Forster told us he returned the e-reader, instead going for the 2024 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition.

In a recent development, our testing also highlighted that when the back panel pops out of place, it can cause frame alignment problems. As a result, I've updated my Kindle review. Previously, I rated the 2026 Kindle as a 5 out of 5 on performance. However, with this back panel issue, I'm changing that to a 4 out of 5.

According to recent reports, when we asked Amazon about the issue, a spokesperson emphasized that the back panel is designed to come off the frame when it's time to replace the battery. If the back panel does come off accidentally, it doesn't mean the device is broken or needs to be replaced.

Industry observers note that testing is an ongoing process here at Mashable. Even after we publish a review, we'll update it as we spend more time with the product, especially if we experience something that changes our first impressions. We want to know how a piece of tech blends into our lives. That's why a comment from my editor on the fresh Kindles stuck with me.

Sources indicate that mashable Tech Editor Timothy Beck Werth went hands-on with the 2026 Kindles at an Amazon preview event. After I completed testing the new basic Kindle, he asked if I'd had trouble removing it from its case. Werth had noticed that during a demo, one of the Kindle bodies briefly popped out of place. It was a relevant question because I actually had experienced that problem, too.

When Amazon sent us the newly introduced Kindle for review, it came with a new fabric cover. I used the device in the case, and all was well until I tried to remove it from stated case. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Removing the Kindle from its fabric cover can be difficult. Sure, that means it's a secure fit, but there was so much resistance that I noticed some bending and strain in the device's frame, as if it were coming apart. Then, once I got the Kindle out of the case, I realized it actually had come apart. The back of the Kindle detached from the screen, revealing the device's innards.

Recent findings suggest that in my three years testing Kindles for Mashable, this has never happened before. No matter how many times I've taken the 2022 or 2024 Kindles out of their cases, I've never once been concerned about the e-readers' structure. But the 2026 Kindles have gone through a major redesign.

Sources indicate that part of that redesign is the removable back panel that allows customers to replace the battery. Unfortunately, I think this change was a little too successful, and now the Kindle's back panel can come apart from the frame accidentally when applying pressure.

We reached out to Amazon for comment, and an Amazon spokesperson relayed that this is part of the redesign: "Your Kindle is designed to open along the edge of the display in order to replace the battery. If the back panel shifts when you remove a case or cover, press it firmly back into place on all four corners and along the edges, and keep reading.".

It has been revealed that having taken the 2026 Kindle in and out of its case several times, I've noticed the frame separation is occurring frequently. The upside is that it's exceptionally easy to put the frame back in place. With a little pressure, the frame clicks back; however, I have noticed some concerns with the power button and gapping around the screen.

The first time this happened, the power button was caught in the frame, and I had to pop it back off to get it to sit right, leaving it scratched. On top of that, even after the screen is clicked back into place, there is gapping along the seam with my review unit, which requires you to apply extra pressure to fix.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, the frame issue does not affect the actual operation of the newly introduced Kindle. It's still a quick-processing e-reader.

We have only encountered this glitch on the basic Kindle model, not the Paperwhite Signature Edition or the latest aluminum-body Kindles. We're still in the process of testing the new Kindle Paperwhite.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gap Inc. on Thursday unveiled Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.

The retailer also said Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday.

Sources indicate that kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.

It has been revealed that "I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter mentioned in a statement.

The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.

Industry observers note that "Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode.".

Dickson said the organization is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.

While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.

Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.

Sources indicate that net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.

Gap also stated it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.

The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.

Dickson remarked in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.

"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson stated.

Here's how the organization performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Recent findings suggest that for the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.

At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. `.

According to recent reports, the company's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.

"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson stated.

It has been revealed that the Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its newly introduced CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.

Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the organization attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.

Dickson mentioned the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.

It has been revealed that "We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he noted. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth.".

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training.
  • Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on problems that matter to them, such as climate protection.
  • It has been revealed that what particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a substantial city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on problems that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

It has been revealed that what particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today.".

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," indicates Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests.".

Industry observers note that the 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

Sources indicate that UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

It has been revealed that this economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30.".

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," claims Brod.

He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

In a recent development, "Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," notes Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

It has been revealed that her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!".

This article was originally published in German.

#70428. Industry News: This smell startup states its AI nose is as good as a human’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1235 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: This smell startup states its AI nose is as good as a human’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in a lab near Newark Airport in Fresh Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth.
  • “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he indicates.
  • In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in a lab near Newark Airport in Fresh Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The firm’s goal, notes founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”.

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he indicates. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”.

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Recent findings suggest that wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko claims, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the firm’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko states. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.).

Sources indicate that the firm also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

In a recent development, osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo introduced, later gave the organization a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

Sources indicate that but not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. In response, Wiltschko says that “human perception isn't a workaround for AI”. “Language models learn from what people have written. Our model learns from what people smell. Smell is ultimately a human experience, so the model has to learn from humans to bridge chemistry and perception. That’s what lets it predict how people will experience a scent as well as the human nose does.”.

Recent findings suggest that michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, states the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

Industry observers note that but even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker indicates. “Smell is super complex. Context is very key for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”.

According to recent reports, in a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.

For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker indicates. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

In a recent development, “There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. "So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Documentary records Catherine taking on Three Peaks challenge and finding ‘sense of hope alongside uncertainty’.

The Princess of Wales has spoken candidly about the impact of her cancer diagnosis in a BBC documentary to be aired later this month.

“Cancer does change you,” Catherine, 44, indicates in the trailer for the 30-minute programme. “It changes your body. It changes you physically, but there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”.

According to recent reports, the film records Catherine taking on the Three Peaks challenge – climbing the three highest mountains in England, Scotland and Wales in 24 hours – and meeting with other people undergoing cancer treatment. Described by the BBC as a “highly personal film”, the documentary, titled Heal, will be shown on BBC One on 29 November.

The trailer emerged as it was reported that King Charles will voluntarily pay “mansion tax” on relevant royal household properties, despite crown exemption. The high-value council tax surcharge, often referred to as a mansion tax, will take effect in 2028 and apply to properties valued at more than £2m.

Catherine was diagnosed with an undisclosed form of cancer in early 2024, for which she received chemotherapy, and by January 2025 unveiled she was in remission.

She was treated at the Royal Marsden hospital in London, a world-leading oncology centre, with funds from the distribution of the documentary, which will also be broadcast in other countries, going to the Royal Marsden cancer charity.

When people successfully finish cancer treatment at the hospital they often ring a bell in celebration. “I didn’t ring the bell,” Catherine says in the trailer, speaking to her brother, James Middleton, as they are walking together.

“Maybe this is your ringing the bell,” he indicates, in reference to her undertaking the Three Peaks challenge and making the programme.

When she completed the challenge in June, 18 months after announcing that the cancer was in remission, she became the first royal to have achieved the feat – climbing Ben Nevis, Scafell Pike and Yr Wyddfa in less than 24 hours, having started on a Saturday evening.

In the programme, which will be introduced by the presenter Kirsty Young, Catherine talks about how she has learned through her recovery to find “a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty”.

Kate Phillips, the BBC’s chief content officer, remarked she hoped the documentary “will resonate with BBC viewers and provide comfort and support to those navigating their own health challenges”.

Flood alerts in place and risk of power cuts as more than 100mm predicted to fall on Dartmoor on Sunday.

Cold snaps are to make way for heavy rain in some parts of the country as the Met Office issued a weather warning for south-west England.

It said there will be a slow-moving band of rain moving across Devon and Cornwall, with more than 100mm due to fall on Dartmoor. The warning will be in place from 6am on Sunday until midnight.

Recent findings suggest that the Met Office said there was a risk of power cuts and added that driving conditions could be difficult. There are active flood alerts in the area.

Cold weather health warnings are in place in northern England until Tuesday morning. The lowest temperature this autumn so far was recored on Friday night.

It has been revealed that north-west and north-east England, and Yorkshire and the Humber, have had yellow alerts issued by the UK Health Security Agency. It suggests there is a risk to vulnerable people and that conditions may put pressure on the health service and people should take care when travelling.

Friday night had the lowest temperature since early January, as Tulloch Bridge in the Highlands recorded -10.6C. It beat this autumn’s record of -8.4C at the same weather station on Thursday.

The Met Office noted there could be a widespread frost across the UK on Saturday night, but there will be warmer and largely drier conditions outside south-west England on Sunday.

The Met Office chief forecaster, Matthew Lehnert, remarked: “Within the warning area, 20-40mm of rain is likely quite widely, but some parts of south Devon and Cornwall could see 60-80mm.

“Over Dartmoor, there is a chance of more than 100mm falling through the day. This slow-moving band of rain will gradually ease on Sunday night, but flooding and travel disruption is possible within the warning area, with south Devon and south Cornwall more likely to see higher totals.

“There is still some uncertainty about where the heaviest rain will fall, so it’s important to stay up to date with the forecast and any warning updates.”.

Add in two highly collectible promo Pokémon cards — Espeon and Umbreon — alongside special Pikachu ex promo cards and all the premium extras (playmat, card sleeves, deck box, etc.), and it’s no wonder that there hasn’t been enough supply to meet the demand.

The accessories and promotional artwork vary between editions, but you’re effectively getting the same level of contents with either box.

#70416. Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (923 w)

Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most crucial temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.
  • Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.
  • It has been revealed that the Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most crucial temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

It has been revealed that the Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

But now there has been a breakthrough.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle.".

Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!".

It has been revealed that nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go.".

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

According to recent reports, digitally fitting the fragments together led to another crucial discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

Industry observers note that the Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Industry observers note that using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

Recent findings suggest that in the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

Greece, however, considers them stolen.

In a recent development, for years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.

A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.

It has been revealed that the studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov. 15, according to data from Rentrak. That's already roughly $290 million, or more than 50%, above its haul for all of 2025.

"They have an identity all their own, and just the mere mention of A24, the recognition that a movie is from A24, gives it instant credibility and provides a must-see factor, no matter what the subject matter," Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, told CNBC.

Skydance co-CEO and Chairman David Ellison cited movie releases from A24 as part of the company's "unmatched portfolio" during its most recent earnings call.

A24 films released this year broke records at the box office, with "Backrooms" becoming the studio's biggest domestic opening to date and "You Can See Everything" notching the biggest documentary opening since "Fahrenheit 9/11" in 2004.

That success has already begun to translate to HBO Max's platform.

When "Backrooms" began streaming on HBO Max, it was the most streamed title on the platform for two weeks, according to Nielsen data. The film was also the fourth overall most streamed title the week it premiered, racking up 226 million minutes of viewing time.

After more than a year of competing bids and regulatory hurdles, Skydance now oversees two of the world's largest streaming platforms: HBO Max and Paramount+.

According to recent reports, the firm prepares to eventually merge the streaming services into a single platform. It will take the first step in that effort by offering a value bundle in early 2027.

The combination of the platforms "will drive stronger engagement and higher lifetime value," co-CEO Ynon Kreiz mentioned on the company's earnings call earlier this month.

In a recent development, paramount Skydance's direct-to-consumer segment, which includes Paramount+ and its free, ad-supported channel, Pluto TV, generated more than $2 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing more than 35% of total revenue for the period. That segment revenue marked an 11% year-over-year increase, with revenue from Paramount+ up 21%.

Sources indicate that the earnings do not reflect the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, since that deal closed after the close of the quarter.

Revenue growth in streaming will be key as it faces the daunting task of managing nearly $80 billion of debt.

The firm has said it expects to realize $6 billion in cost savings over the next three years and has put a particular focus on consolidating its operations and streamlining its marketing spend.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Local MP says legitimate criticisms of asylum housing prepares are being co-opted by opposition parties ‘stirring up racial discord’.
  • Residents of a Suffolk village have voted to “leave the UK” in a referendum held in response to government plans to house 930 asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.
  • Industry observers note that approximately 500 people in Barnham were eligible to take part in the symbolic vote on Saturday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Local MP says legitimate criticisms of asylum housing prepares are being co-opted by opposition parties ‘stirring up racial discord’.

Residents of a Suffolk village have voted to “leave the UK” in a referendum held in response to government plans to house 930 asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.

Industry observers note that approximately 500 people in Barnham were eligible to take part in the symbolic vote on Saturday. There were 257 votes for independence, 16 against and one spoiled ballot.

After the vote, Helen Beck, the chair of Barnham Residents’ Association, mentioned Barnham’s flag would be a stone-curlew on a “Suffolk blue background”.

RAF Barnham was one of three Ministry of Defence sites named in June by the government as potential locations for newly introduced developments to house asylum seekers.

A similar referendum was held in Piddington, Oxfordshire in September, with residents also voting to leave the UK amid plans to house more than 1,000 migrants at another former military base.

It has been revealed that in Barnham, the prepares have prompted protests outside the site. The referendum asked residents whether they supported seeking a “crown dependency status”, which is a similar system to that of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man.

John Bauer, the parish council chair, noted this would allow the village to “retain loyalty to the crown” but remove itself from Home Office jurisdiction.

In a recent development, while in opposition the Labour party had attacked the Conservative policy to house asylum seekers on military bases; once in government, however, the party backtracked. The Conservatives have also reversed their position, with Kemi Badenoch telling frustrated villagers “the Conservative party is on your side”.

“We know that the problem of the boats needs to stop and we have got a plan to stop it,” she mentioned on Friday.

Earlier this month, it was revealed construction company Kier would design the fresh camp at RAF Barnham.

Before Saturday’s vote Labour’s Dr Peter Prinsley, the local MP, said he was against the development of the site. Prinsley said the plans resembled a “concentration camp”, and warned that planning permission may be difficult to attain due to environmental concerns about rare species living in the area – in particular, stone-curlews – with previous development applications nearby having been turned down.

“This is a symbolic referendum,” Prinsley remarked. “It’s not going to produce a binding result. I’m expecting that [the result] will be hugely in favour of becoming a crown dependency. There are 500 electors, so I’m expecting it to be 500 – nil.”.

He added that the government “is doing an awful lot to deal with the irregular migration problem”, and highlighted that net migration may come down to “more or less zero by the end of the year”.

According to recent reports, but he added that he didn’t think “the large army camps in remote locations are ever likely to be appropriate for the distribution of people seeking asylum. The fact is that people who arrive here on small boats are not illegal migrants. They are people who are seeking asylum. Our political opponents have described these people as ‘illegals, criminals, rapists’, and all sorts of things that they’re not. They’re just people who have arrived on small boats. The government is getting a grip on this problem, but it’s a complicated problem.”.

He said the proposed Barnham site had particular challenges which may make it unsuitable. “It’s a remote location without any pedestrian access, it’s on a very hazardous main road. When it was used as military accommodation there were serious accidents on that road.

“It’s also a site of special scientific interest because it is the nesting site for stone-curlews, which will make any planning application very difficult – even a government planning application – because these are worldwide protections.”.

He suggested “disused office blocks in some of the larger cities” may be more appropriate places to house asylum seekers, with more local services available.

Sources indicate that “It feels like a concentration camp,” Prinsley added. “It doesn’t feel like a place that has a compassionate approach to people who are fleeing persecution and are being processed for asylum.”.

He also said legitimate criticism of the plans had been co-opted by opposition parties who are aiming to “stir up racial discord”.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “We recognise the strength of feeling in local communities and are listening carefully to the concerns being raised.

“The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election.

In a recent development, “This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to reduce the impact on local communities.”.

Latest Update: COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's looks to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.
  • But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.
  • "We are extremely concerned about the situation," mentioned a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's looks to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," mentioned a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this glitch, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions.".

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action prepares for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report covers climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," stated a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Industry observers note that disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," remarked a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

"We have no time to lose," mentioned an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive.".

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake.".

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science.".

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

In a recent development, the IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the intends to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

Industry observers note that at least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment.".

It has been revealed that the presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

Recent findings suggest that the presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

This article was originally written in German.

#70405. The Manosphere Isn’t Ready for Brothercore
